title: You don’t fall into rebellion overnight. It grows quietly, like a fracture beneath polished strength, like a whisper you entertained a little too long. The story of Absalom didn’t begin at the city gate—it began in a wounded heart that was never healed.
paragraphs: You don’t fall into rebellion overnight. It grows quietly, like a fracture beneath polished strength, like a whisper you entertained a little too long. The story of Absalom didn’t begin at the city gate—it began in a wounded heart that was never healed.

The palace of David looked whole from the outside. Victories, songs, honor. But inside, something was rotting. Sin had already entered the house, and it didn’t leave when the moment passed. It stayed. It spread.
It started with injustice.

Absalom’s sister, Tamar, was violated by their brother Amnon. And David… did nothing. No judgment. No justice. Silence where righteousness should have thundered. You can almost feel it—the confusion, the anger, the quiet storm building in Absalom’s chest. Because when authority refuses to act, bitterness steps in to take its place.
“Then Absalom spoke to his brother Amnon neither good nor bad: for Absalom hated Amnon…” (2 Samuel 13:22)
Read that again.
Hatred doesn’t always shout. Sometimes it waits.

Two years passed. Not healing—waiting. Then Absalom took justice into his own hands and had Amnon killed. It felt right. It felt justified. But it was still sin. And sin, even when it feels righteous, always plants deeper chains.

He fled. Exile followed. Distance grew. But here’s what most people don’t realize—distance doesn’t heal what pride refuses to confront. Absalom returned eventually, but the fracture between him and David was never truly restored. There was no repentance. No reconciliation rooted in truth. Just surface peace covering unresolved fire.
And that fire found a new expression.
Control.
Influence.
Power.
Absalom began to position himself at the gates of the city, where ordinary people came seeking justice. He intercepted them, listened to their complaints, and slowly turned their hearts.
“Oh that I were made judge in the land…” (2 Samuel 15:4)
He didn’t say it all at once. He didn’t need to.
He was strategic.
Calculated.
Charming.
“And Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel.” (2 Samuel 15:6)
God saw it.
And deep down—he knew.
This wasn’t just political ambition. This was a son trying to replace a father he no longer trusted. A man trying to build authority without submission. A soul that chose image over repentance.
You’ve seen this before.
Maybe not in a kingdom—but in your own life.

When you were hurt… and instead of surrendering it to God, you held it. When you were overlooked… and instead of trusting His timing, you started positioning yourself. When correction came… and you rejected it, but still wanted influence.
That’s where Absalom was.
And it led him to a moment where he declared himself king.
Rebellion doesn’t feel evil when you’re inside it. It feels justified. Necessary. Even righteous. But Scripture doesn’t bend to your emotions.
“Rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft…” (1 Samuel 15:23)
That’s not symbolic language. That’s exposure.
Because rebellion is ultimately a rejection of God’s authority. It says, “My way is better.” It crowns self and dethrones truth.
And Absalom paid for it.

The rebellion rose fast—but it collapsed even faster. David fled, weeping. A kingdom shaken. A family torn. And in the end, Absalom found himself hanging from a tree, caught by the very thing that symbolized his pride—his hair.
No army could save him.
No charm could rescue him.
No strategy could reverse what sin had already set in motion.
“And they took three darts in their hand, and thrust them through the heart of Absalom…” (2 Samuel 18:14)
That’s how it ended.
Not with a crown.
But with judgment.
And somewhere in the distance, David cried, “O my son Absalom… would God I had died for thee…”
Feel that.
A broken father.
A lost son.
All because sin was never dealt with at the root.
Originally written by Gospel Warrior
But this isn’t just history. This is a mirror.
Because the same pattern still lives today.
Unhealed wounds.
Unconfessed sin.
Rejected authority.
Self-exaltation.
And eventually… separation.
But there’s another Son who hung on a tree.
Not because of His rebellion—but because of yours.
Jesus Christ didn’t seize a throne. He surrendered Himself. Where Absalom tried to take a kingdom, Jesus laid down His life to redeem one.
“Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures…” (1 Corinthians 15:3)
This is where the story can change.
Because your rebellion doesn’t have to end in destruction. It can end in surrender.
Repentance isn’t weakness. It’s the doorway back.
Grace isn’t earned. It’s given.
But you have to come honestly.
No more positioning.
No more pretending.
No more silent resentment hidden behind spiritual language.
God already saw it.
You knew.
And yet—He still calls.
Let it press. Let it confront. Say it plainly if you have to: “I’ve been resisting God.”
